abstract: First issue of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's monthly AI Economic Indicators update, published November 18, 2026, with latest data through October 2026. A two-page brief summarising four dashboards: the Canaries Dashboard (employment by age and AI exposure, built with ADP Research), the Adoption Monitor (generative AI use at work), the GDP-B Surplus Observer (consumer surplus from generative AI tools), and the Transformation Tracker, renamed from the Takeoff Tracker. Its headline is an age split: 'Over the last year, employment rose for workers 35+ but fell for those under 35, most steeply in AI-exposed jobs.' The early-career reading deteriorated — ages 22-25 in the most AI-exposed jobs are at -4.2 percent year over year for October 2026, against -3.5 percent a month earlier and -3.3 percent six months earlier — while the macro picture did not move at all.
keyFindings: Canaries Dashboard, October 2026: employment change from a year earlier for ages 22-25 in the most AI-exposed jobs is -4.2 percent, against -3.5 percent one month earlier and -3.3 percent six months earlier. The steepest reading the dashboard has published and a clear deterioration over the past month.
Across the wider young band, employment fell 2.2 percent year over year for ages 22-34 and rose 0.4 percent for ages 35 and older. Employment fell for every age group under 35.
In the most AI-exposed jobs, employment of 22- to 25-year-olds has been below its year-earlier level every month since October 2023 - three full years of continuous year-over-year decline.

Transformation Tracker (September 2026): 3 of 12 macro indicators are well above their pre-2020 trends, unchanged from one month and six months earlier. All three measure capital - the shares of IT in business equipment, of software and R&D in business capital, and of capital in national income. Capital's share of income is given as 41.7 percent in 2024.

The brief states plainly that 'Signs of an economy-wide AI transformation are limited so far: GDP and productivity are growing at their usual pace.' The early-career labour signal and the macro signal continue to point in opposite directions.

Adoption Monitor: 45 percent of employed US adults use generative AI for their job as of a May 2026 survey, against 43 percent three months earlier and 35 percent a year earlier. This is the Bick, Blandin and Deming Real-Time Population Survey, tracked on this site as its own recurring series, and the May 2026 vintage is older than the reading already plotted on genai-work-adoption.

GDP-B Surplus Observer: 183 billion dollars is the annual amount 127 million US users would collectively need to be paid to give up generative AI, as of July 2026, against 172 billion four months earlier and 116 billion a year earlier. Consumer surplus rather than a labour-market quantity, and not mapped to any prediction graph.
methodology: Monthly brief summarising four Lab dashboards. The Canaries figures come from anonymized ADP payroll records for a balanced sample of firms using ADP services, tracking the same firms over time, with occupations partitioned by AI exposure scores from Eloundou et al. (2024); the Lab describes it as an early-warning signal and not a measure of economy-wide employment. The Adoption Monitor synthesises survey evidence, here Bick, Blandin and Deming. The Surplus Observer uses the Brynjolfsson et al. GDP-B willingness-to-accept design. The Transformation Tracker assembles 12 macro indicators from BEA, FRED, EIA and Federal Reserve sources and compares each against its pre-2020 trend. The brief is published at https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/YYYY/MM/AIEI_MU_<Mon><YY>.pdf; AIEI_MU_Nov26.pdf is the first such file and probes for Aug26, Sep26 and Oct26 return 404, so no earlier issue of this format was missed.
qualifiers: The -4.2 percent figure is a raw year-over-year change in the level of employment among ADP client firms, not the most-exposed-versus-least-exposed differential that early-career-employment-decline plots, so it is recorded as a directional signal rather than a data point. The brief itself is explicit about the limits: 'This pattern alone does not show AI caused these declines' and 'AI exposure measures how much AI could apply to a job's tasks, which may differ from actual AI adoption.' The ADP sample skews to medium and large private-sector employers and is not nationally representative; the balanced-firm design excludes entry and exit. Three of the four dashboards report different as-of dates in the same brief - Canaries October 2026, Transformation Tracker September 2026, Surplus Observer July 2026, Adoption Monitor May 2026 - so the brief's publication date is not the reference date for any single figure. Overlays drawn from it are dated to the reference period of the figure cited, not to publication.
